outcome: Nothing in the sources has settled or moved whether a same-parity betrothed pair exists: none has been found or excluded since 26 January 2024. The in-window events are formalisations of the question (a January 2026 Lean paper on the definitions; February 2026 and August 2026 entries in DeepMind's formal-conjectures repository, the second correcting a misstatement), and the problem remains open.
problem_asks: (1) Whether there exists a pair of betrothed numbers m and n, where betrothed means s(m) = n + 1 and s(n) = m + 1 with s the proper-divisor (aliquot) sum; equivalently sigma(m) = sigma(n) = m + n + 1 with sigma the sum-of-divisors function. (2) Whether such a pair can have m and n of the same parity (both even, or both odd). This is one existence question with a yes-or-no answer. It does not ask for bounds, counts, a classification, or the parity of the known pairs. Reading note: the statement says 'pairs' without saying distinct. m = n gives the quasiperfect case sigma(n) = 2n + 1. The February 2026 Lean statement did not require m != n; the August 2026 correction added it, so the distinct reading is the one the formal repository now uses.

events.what_happened: First pairs found by hand or early computation, reported only secondarily: (48, 75) attributed to Nasir (1946); the next pairs to Makowski (1960); Garcia (1968, 'Numeros casi amigos y casi sociables') found further pairs and named them quasi-amicable; Lal and Forbes (1971) also enumerated pairs. Sources are the OEIS A005276 comment by Amiram Eldar and a search snippet of Pollack 2011. The primary papers were not opened.
events.delivers: Lists the first handful of pairs, starting with (48, 75). No parity statement is recorded in the secondary sources. Restricted to listing pairs, so it says nothing about whether a same-parity pair exists.
events.remains: The whole problem. Same-parity existence is not addressed.
events.directly_checkable: The pair (48, 75) can be checked by hand: sigma(48) = 124 = sigma(75) = 48 + 75 + 1.
events.doubts: Secondary attribution only; primary papers not seen.
events.direction: Neutral. Exhibits the first pairs, all of opposite parity.
events.object: The pair (48, 75): sigma(48) = sigma(75) = 124 = 48 + 75 + 1. Explicit and checkable by hand. Not a same-parity pair.

events.what_happened: P. Hagis Jr. and G. Lord, 'Quasi-amicable numbers', Mathematics of Computation 31(138) (1977), 608-611, DOI 10.1090/S0025-5718-1977-0434939-3. Computational enumeration of pairs: the first 46 pairs (per OEIS), later extended to 107 by Beck and Najar (per a search snippet). The 2013 OEIS comment by Harvey P. Dale and the Wikipedia references attribute to this paper the same-parity lower bound 'a > 10^10' for the smaller member. The paper was not opened: the AMS page returned HTTP 403.
events.delivers: Enumeration of pairs up to a search limit. Per secondary report only, a lower bound of 10^10 on the smaller member of any same-parity pair. I have not seen the paper's statement, so I cannot say whether this is a theorem or a computational observation.
events.remains: Existence of a same-parity pair (not addressed by the enumeration).

events.what_happened: Paul Pollack, 'Quasi-amicable numbers are rare', Journal of Integer Sequences 14 (2011), Article 11.5.2. Proves that the set of n lying in some quasi-amicable pair has asymptotic density zero. The journal page gives received 26 Nov 2010, revised 16 Apr 2011, published 21 Apr 2011. The paper says previous theoretical work was very limited. NOT OPENED: the EMIS HTML returned HTTP 503 and the cs.uwaterloo PDF was not readable through my fetch. The abstract is taken from a search snippet of the EMIS page.
events.delivers: Density-zero statement about the integers that belong to quasi-amicable pairs (per the abstract snippet). That is a statement about how rare members of pairs are; the snippet says nothing about the parity of the two members. Full text unread.
events.remains: The same-parity existence question, and every other part of problem_asks.

events.what_happened: Harvey P. Dale, comment on OEIS A003503 dated 7 Apr 2013. States that it has been shown that all known betrothed pairs have opposite parity, and that if a < b are of the same parity then a > 10^10, citing the Hagis and Lord paper. Comment only, with no derivation.
events.delivers: Restates a size bound (smaller member greater than 10^10) for same-parity pairs, attributed to Hagis and Lord. No existence result.
events.remains: Existence of a same-parity pair, and any part of problem_asks other than the size bound.
events.doubts: Unreferenced restatement. Its 'it has been shown' rests on the cited 1977 paper, which I have not read.
events.direction: No existence result. A size bound on a hypothetical smallest counterexample.

events.what_happened: David A. Corneth, comment on OEIS A003503 dated 26 Jan 2019. Shows sigma(k) = sigma(m) for any betrothed pair (k, m). If k and m are both odd, both are squares. If both are even, each is a square or twice a square. Concludes that if k and m are a betrothed pair of the same parity, the minimal term is greater than 2*10^14, 'using inspection and the results above'. Also gives a PARI program (truncated in what I saw). Comment only, not a paper.
events.delivers: Under the comment's argument, any same-parity betrothed pair has minimal term above 2*10^14. This is a size bound on a hypothetical counterexample. It establishes neither existence nor non-existence. The square-structure lemmas are the comment's own; I did not re-derive them.
events.remains: Existence: whether any same-parity pair exists at all, and whether one exists above the stated bound.
events.directly_checkable: Candidate pairs are checkable by computing sigma. The 'inspection' step is not documented in the comment as I read it.
events.doubts: The bound rests on 'inspection' with no documented search range or method. The PARI snippet is truncated. I did not re-derive the parity lemmas. Wikipedia (last edited 14 Mar 2026) still gives 10^13 and does not cite this comment. No source I found cites it.
events.direction: Cuts neither way on existence. It raises the claimed size of any same-parity pair, if one exists, well above the 10^10 and 10^13 figures elsewhere.

events.what_happened: Amiram Eldar, comment on OEIS A005276 dated 9 Mar 2024. Historical remarks only: first pair (48, 75) found by Nasir (1946); Hagis and Lord (1977) found the first 46 pairs, after Garcia (1968); Beck and Wajar found six more (the comment dates this 1971) and the next 33 (1993), missing two pairs in the process. No new pair and no parity statement.
events.delivers: Historical restatement only. No new pair, no parity result, no bound.
events.direction: Neutral. Discounted: it reports history, not progress.

events.what_happened: Zhipeng Chen, Haolun Tang and Jingyi Zhan, 'Formalization of Amicable Numbers Theory', arXiv:2601.07444 (cs.LO), submitted 12 Jan 2026. A Lean 4 / Mathlib formalisation of amicable-number theory. It defines betrothed numbers as s(m) = n + 1 and s(n) = m + 1, verifies (48, 75) and (140, 195) computationally, and lists betrothed numbers and 'parity constraint theorems' among its extensions. The authors state the formalisation has zero sorry placeholders (sections 1, 5.1, 6).
events.revisions: v1 only, submitted 12 Jan 2026 (arXiv abstract page).
events.delivers: A formal definition of betrothed pairs, plus machine verification that (48, 75) and (140, 195) are betrothed. No new pair. No result on the parity of betrothed pairs: per the summarising read of the HTML (section 3.7.4), its parity theorems are stated for amicable pairs (IsAmicablePair), not betrothed pairs.
events.remains: Everything the problem asks: whether a same-parity betrothed pair exists.

machine_checked.note: Authors' claim (sections 1, 5.1, 6). Not verified by me. The paper's repository https://github.com/chainstart/amicable-numbers (2 commits, Apache 2.0) lists amicable-number files (Amicable.lean, AmicableLib, Amicable/Basic.lean) and no betrothed content, so the betrothed code the paper describes was not located.

events.directly_checkable: The pairs (48, 75) and (140, 195) can be checked by hand against sigma.
events.doubts: (a) Section 3.7.4 says the parity theorems are formalised 'without proof' and also 'proven using 2-adic valuation arguments' in consecutive sentences. (b) Per the summarising read, section 3.7.5 attributes a search bound to 'Pedersen (2003)', which is not in the reference list. (c) The betrothed code was not found in the repository. (d) The zero-sorry claim is the authors' own. None of these bears directly on the existence question.
events.direction: No direction on the question. Confirms known pairs; does not address parity of betrothed pairs.
events.object: The formal definition of betrothed pairs and verified instances (48, 75) and (140, 195). Not a candidate same-parity pair.

events.what_happened: Two issues opened 10 Feb 2026 by GitHub user franzhusch: #2243 'Do betrothed number pairs with the same parity exist?' and #2246 'Infinitude of Betrothed Numbers'. Both closed as completed by PR #2264 'feat(Wikipedia): Conjectures about Betrothed Numbers', merged 15 Feb 2026 by mo271 (commit 6399d12). The new file FormalConjectures/Wikipedia/BetrothedNumbers.lean defines IsBetrothed (sigma 1 m = m + n + 1 and sigma 1 n = m + n + 1), proves IsBetrothed 48 75 and symmetry, and states same_parity_betrothed (answer(sorry) <-> exists m n, IsBetrothed m n and (Even m <-> Even n)) and infinitely_many_betrothed. Both are tagged research open, AMS 11, and both are sorry-proofed. As the August 2026 issue reports, the merged same_parity statement did not require m != n.

events.remains: All of problem_asks. The existence question is the sorry-proofed statement.

events.what_happened: Akira Toyohara, Ye Tao and Siqiong Yao, 'Every quasiperfect number has at least eight distinct prime factors', arXiv:2608.02066 (math.NT), submitted 3 Aug 2026. disputes.summary: Stated bounds for a same-parity pair disagree. Wikipedia (raw wikitext: '10<sup>13</sup>', no inline citation seen) says any same-parity pair must exceed 10^13. Dale (2013) on OEIS, citing Hagis and Lord (1977), says the smaller member must exceed 10^10. Corneth (2019) on OEIS gives a minimal term above 2*10^14 'using inspection'. An older Wikipedia mirror gives 10^10. These are different claims about the smallest possible counterexample and I have not found which is current or verified.
Beck and Wajar's 1977 paper is dated 1971 in one OEIS remark and 1977 in the references. Its co-author is spelled Wajar in its byline and Najar in several references.

summary: Searched 50 times (WebSearch, standard mode except two extended runs) and opened the following: Wikipedia (rendered and raw wikitext); OEIS A003503 and A005276; arXiv 2601.07444 and 2608.02066; MathWorld; Futility Closet; the formal-conjectures issues #2243, #2246 and #4998, PRs #2264 and #4999, and the Lean file BetrothedNumbers.lean; and the amicable-numbers repository chainstart/amicable-numbers. Nothing found settles, or moves in a way that bears on existence, the question whether a betrothed pair with both members of the same parity exists. None has been found or excluded. Known pairs all have opposite parity (Wikipedia; OEIS; Futility Closet, which says the question is open). The size bounds are the only quantitative content: 10^10 (Dale 2013, attributing to Hagis and Lord 1977), 2*10^14 (Corneth 2019, minimal term, 'using inspection'), and 10^13 (Wikipedia, uncited). These constrain a hypothetical counterexample; they decide nothing about existence, and the problem does not ask for them. The in-window events are formalisations and one misstatement fix. (i) A January 2026 Lean paper formalises amicable numbers and defines betrothed pairs, verifying (48, 75) and (140, 195). Its 'parity constraint theorems' are stated for amicable pairs, not betrothed pairs. (ii) In February 2026 franzhusch opened issues #2243 and #2246, merged by mo271 in PR #2264. The repository states the same-parity question as a sorry-proofed open Lean statement. Its AI disclosures are 'This issue was generated by an AI agent and reviewed by me' (issue) and 'Formalization done with the help of Claude Opus 4.6' (PR). (iii) On 15-16 Aug 2026, Kuberwastaken's issue #4998 and PR #4999 corrected same_parity_betrothed to require m != n, so quasiperfect numbers no longer satisfy it. The issue reports a sieve to 5*10^6 finding 35 betrothed pairs, all of opposite parity, and says it decides nothing. Its AI disclosure is 'prepared with AI assistance (Claude, Anthropic) for the source audit, the sieve computation, and drafting'. On AI: no AI system is credited with any mathematical result on this problem. I have not placed any system in ai.systems, because the contributions I found are statement formalisation, source checking, a computation with no result, and drafting. Section 5.4 excludes those from ai.systems, though all of them count as involvement. none_found is false for the formal-conjectures events and the August correction, and true for the rest. Where a call was close: (a) whether formal statements count as events bearing on the problem; I recorded them and they deliver nothing, so the judging pass can discount them. (b) Whether Corneth's bound moves a quantity the problem names: the problem asks only existence, and the bound is on a hypothetical minimum, so I treat it as a bound rather than a resolution. (c) Whether a model's role in writing a formal statement is AI involvement in the mathematics: I say it is involvement but not in the result, which is the reading §5.4 gives for formalisation, and I flag it in the event for the later pass. Current status signal: as of the 16 Aug 2026 merge, the DeepMind repository still tags same_parity_betrothed as research open with a sorry proof. Futility Closet (29 Sep 2025) and Wikipedia (last edited 14 Mar 2026) state the question as open and cite nothing new; I read them but did not record them as events, since they are digests and not work bearing on the problem. Adjacent, discounted: the Toyohara et al. quasiperfect bound (3 Aug 2026), recorded as an event because the m = n case is quasiperfect.
competing_reading: The strongest reading against the record: Corneth's 2019 comment is a genuine partial result on this question, not a computation. Its square-structure lemmas restrict any same-parity pair to a very sparse family and put the least such pair above 2*10^14. If the argument holds, it is the most substantive content the record holds, and it falls before the window, so it does not count as since-2024 progress. In the other direction, one could say the 2026 formal-conjectures entries are not research at all and should be discounted as no-events; I recorded them because they are the only in-window items that address this question directly, and they deliver nothing. A third reading would take the Lean paper's 'parity constraint theorems' as bearing on betrothed pairs. Its own text, read through the summarising fetch, says they concern amicable pairs.
what_would_settle_it: For existence: a same-parity pair (directly checkable by computing sigma(m) and sigma(n)), or a proof that same parity is impossible. For the bounds: the 1977 Hagis and Lord text (the source of the 10^10 claim); the origin of Wikipedia's 10^13 bound; a refereed or written-up version of Corneth's argument and its search. For the record's gaps: Guy's Unsolved Problems in Number Theory, section B5, to confirm the problem's wording (I saw only OEIS citations to it); Pollack 2011 in full; the Lean paper's PDF and any betrothed code; the sieve code and output for issue #4998 and the PR #4999 diff.
